It determines who controls the hours around that work—the hours in which life has to happen.

An unpredictable schedule does more than create inconvenience. It makes every other commitment conditional (the hours promised to children, doctors, classes, second jobs, or sleep). A worker may technically be free when off the clock, but that freedom shrinks if software can summon, dismiss, or rearrange them with little warning. The employer doesn't need to issue an explicit order. Uncertainty does the work—keeping the worker available without paying for the whole span of availability.

That is why unpredictability is a form of control. Control isn't only the power to say “work now.” It is also the power to prevent someone from confidently committing elsewhere. The threat of a late change reaches beyond the workplace (and sometimes beyond the worker's own phone). It occupies time before a shift begins and after one appears to end. The schedule becomes a fence whose location can move at the owner's convenience.

Consider the ordinary test: if you receive a closing shift tonight and an opening shift tomorrow, can the intervening hours really be called yours? A company may answer that no one is forced to accept added hours. But refusal can carry consequences (including fewer future shifts, lost favor, or the risk of being labeled unavailable). Even when none of those consequences is written down, the software gives management a one-sided option—that choice has value, and the worker is providing it.

Software can make this control look neutral. An alert arrives from a system, not a supervisor (a worker sees a screen rather than the person who set the rule). Yet code does not choose the policy. Employers decide how much notice matters, whether workers can decline changes, and who absorbs forecasting errors. Automation can hide those choices behind a clean interface—but it cannot make the choices fair.

What would a fairer rule require? First, posted schedules should carry a real notice period (a manager could still request a change, but not command one without consequence). Second, workers should be able to refuse last-minute additions without retaliation. Third, employers should pay for changes they initiate: a premium recognizes that disrupted time has a cost. Emergencies can be defined narrowly. Chronic understaffing can't be allowed to dress itself as an emergency.

Organizing must reach the software and the rulebook behind it. Bargaining over wages while leaving scheduling systems untouched misses a major source of power (the right to change the plan after everyone else has arranged life around it). Workers and organisers can demand audit access, records of changes, clear assignment rules, and enforceable remedies. We should ask who configured the system, who benefits from each setting, and who bears the mistake. If the answer is always the worker, that's not efficiency. It's transferred risk.

The point isn't to freeze every workplace into a rigid timetable. Some operations need adjustment, and some workers want ways to trade or pick up shifts (and any agreement should preserve that choice). The point is that flexibility must run both ways. That floor doesn't restrict voluntary flexibility; it separates a genuine choice from a demand. A system will not be fair merely because its commands arrive quickly and its calculations remain invisible. Scheduling software that changes shifts at short notice is usually sold as efficiency. It promises to match staffing to demand, reduce idle time, and fill gaps quickly. Those goals can be legitimate. But the practical cost is concealed: the employer gains flexibility by taking it from workers. A schedule isn't merely information about work (what time to arrive and when to leave). It determines who controls the hours around that work—the hours in which life has to happen.

An unpredictable schedule does more than create inconvenience. It makes every other commitment conditional (the hours promised to children, doctors, classes, second jobs, or sleep). A worker may technically be free when off the clock, but that freedom shrinks if software can summon, dismiss, or rearrange them with little warning. The employer doesn't need to issue an explicit order. Uncertainty does the work—keeping the worker available without paying for the whole span of availability.

That is why unpredictability is a form of control. Control isn't only the power to say “work now.” It is also the power to prevent someone from confidently committing elsewhere. The threat of a late change reaches beyond the workplace (and sometimes beyond the worker's own phone). It occupies time before a shift begins and after one appears to end. The schedule becomes a fence whose location can move at the owner's convenience.

Consider the ordinary test: if you receive a closing shift tonight and an opening shift tomorrow, can the intervening hours really be called yours? A company may answer that no one is forced to accept added hours. But refusal can carry consequences (including fewer future shifts, lost favor, or the risk of being labeled unavailable). Even when none of those consequences is written down, the software gives management a one-sided option—that choice has value, and the worker is providing it.

Software can make this control look neutral. An alert arrives from a system, not a supervisor (a worker sees a screen rather than the person who set the rule). Yet code does not choose the policy. Employers decide how much notice matters, whether workers can decline changes, and who absorbs forecasting errors. Automation can hide those choices behind a clean interface—but it cannot make the choices fair.

What would a fairer rule require? First, posted schedules should carry a real notice period (a manager could still request a change, but not command one without consequence). Second, workers should be able to refuse last-minute additions without retaliation. Third, employers should pay for changes they initiate: a premium recognizes that disrupted time has a cost. Emergencies can be defined narrowly. Chronic understaffing can't be allowed to dress itself as an emergency.

Organizing must reach the software and the rulebook behind it. Bargaining over wages while leaving scheduling systems untouched misses a major source of power (the right to change the plan after everyone else has arranged life around it). Workers and organisers can demand audit access, records of changes, clear assignment rules, and enforceable remedies. We should ask who configured the system, who benefits from each setting, and who bears the mistake. If the answer is always the worker, that's not efficiency. It's transferred risk.

The point isn't to freeze every workplace into a rigid timetable. Some operations need adjustment, and some workers want ways to trade or pick up shifts (and any agreement should preserve that choice). The point is that flexibility must run both ways. That floor doesn't restrict voluntary flexibility; it separates a genuine choice from a demand. A system will not be fair merely because its commands arrive quickly and its calculations remain invisible. Employers should disclose the rules and pay for disruption; unions should bargain over notice, refusal, and records; lawmakers should set a floor where bargaining cannot reach. Our time should not become an employer's reserve supply just because an app can redraw it.
